justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook anchored around the current price level, with only modest drift upward over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 24.9 is essentially a mean-reversion assumption — absent any major catalyst, prices tend to stay close to where they are, and the tight interval reflects that short-term noise is bounded. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 24.95, acknowledging that small directional momentum or carry effects could edge the price marginally up, but without strong conviction in either direction. At the one-month horizon, the 25.1 estimate reflects a mild upward drift assumption, consistent with typical long-run tendencies in the underlying asset class, though the wide confidence interval communicates genuine uncertainty about where the price will settle over that longer window.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a direct reflection of the compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans just one full unit (24.4 to 25.4), consistent with typical daily volatility. By one week, the interval widens to 2.3 units, capturing the possibility of a trend developing or reversing. By one month, the interval spans 5.2 units, reflecting the realistic range of outcomes driven by macro shifts, sentiment changes, and supply-demand dynamics that can emerge over four weeks.

The primary sources of uncertainty include macroeconomic data releases (inflation prints, employment reports, central bank communications), which can shift risk appetite abruptly. Liquidity conditions and positioning also matter — if the market is crowded in one direction, a sharp reversal is plausible even without a fundamental catalyst.

Specific tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise policy shift from a major central bank, a geopolitical shock, or an unexpected earnings or economic data release that dramatically reprices growth expectations. On the upside, a coordinated stimulus announcement or better-than-expected economic data could push prices well above 27.7 within a month. On the downside, a credit event, sudden risk-off move, or sharp commodity disruption could push prices below 22.5. These low-probability but high-impact scenarios are the primary reasons the tails of my distribution carry meaningful weight even when the point estimates appear benign.
